title: Teach us to pray (Luke 11:1–4)
hookLine: Luke's shorter version of the Lord's Prayer

cards: Luke keeps showing Jesus at prayer: at his baptism, all night before choosing the twelve, on the mountain when his face changed.

Today he is praying in a certain place, and his friends wait a little way off until he finishes. When he stops, one of them asks a question. Not about miracles, not about the kingdom, not about who's the greatest.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." John the Baptist had taught his followers to pray; now they want to be taught too. What Jesus gives is short.

The King James text of Luke reads much like Matthew's; some modern Bibles print Luke's version shorter still, opening with one word, Father, and then five requests. Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come.
Bread for each day. Forgiveness. And protection from the time of trial.
Two small differences from Matthew are worth hearing. Luke's bread line is "Give us day by day our daily bread."

teach.h: DAY BY DAY, NOT A STOCKPILE.
teach.b: Day by day: not a stockpile, a habit. And where Matthew says debts, Luke says: "And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us."
Sins for what we've done, debts for what others owe us; Matthew uses debts for both.

teach.h: THE CLOSING LINE ISN'T IN LUKE.
teach.b: One more surprise: the closing line, for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, isn't in Luke at all, even in the King James. The King James has it in Matthew.

Some churches say it straight after the prayer; in the Catholic Mass it comes a moment later, after another short prayer by the priest. So a prayer said in churches today began as a short answer to a simple request.

how: Christians say the Lord's Prayer in worship and at home, usually in Matthew's wording; some churches add the closing doxology straight after it, while the Catholic Mass places it after a short prayer by the priest.

games.q: you've just watched Jesus pray in a quiet place. he finishes and looks up. what do you ask?
o: nothing. you wait for him to speak.
games.why: one disciple asks: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." the answer is a short prayer, not a lecture.

practice: If you pray, say Luke's King James lines slowly, one per breath, with long gaps: hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; give us day by day our daily bread; and forgive us our sins, for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us; and lead us not into temptation.
If you don't pray, take just one of those requests, bread, forgiveness or protection, and sit with the one that names something you actually need today.

wordCard.voice: Father. The one word Luke's shorter version of the Lord's Prayer opens with, a disciple's request after watching Jesus pray, answered with just five requests after it.

orig.note: Greek: Father, spoken to God directly. some modern Bibles open Luke's prayer with this one word.
